Asset Depletion Loans: How to Get a Mortgage With No Income

The live post shows its featured photo behind this title

Retired, between jobs or living off investments? Your savings can count as income.

By Paul Hankins, Founder, CEO and Broker, NMLS #281393

An asset depletion loan lets you qualify for a mortgage with your savings instead of a paycheck. The lender adds up your accounts, sets aside what you need to buy the home, and turns the rest into a monthly income figure. That figure counts just like a salary.

It is built for people with money in the bank but little income on paper:

  • retirees living on savings;
  • people who sold a business or a property;
  • people between jobs or taking time off;
  • investors who live off their accounts.

How asset depletion works

Lenders use a simple formula:

(Your eligible assets − down payment − closing costs − reserves) ÷ a set number of months = your monthly qualifying income

Reserves are the savings a lender wants you to still have after closing. Whatever is left after the purchase gets spread over the months, and that monthly amount is your income for the loan.

The number of months makes a big difference. Fannie Mae's version divides by the months in the loan: 360 for a 30-year mortgage. Some of the lenders we work with divide by just 60. That 60 is only used to figure your income. Your mortgage itself is still a normal home loan.

An example. Linda is 66. She sold her business and has $1.4 million in savings and investments, but no paycheck. After her down payment, closing costs and reserves, $900,000 of eligible assets are left. A lender that divides by 360 months counts $2,500 a month as her income. A lender that divides by 60 months counts $15,000 a month. Same savings, very different buying power. That is why the lender you choose matters.

What counts as an asset

Lenders don't count every dollar the same way. Cash counts in full. Stocks and retirement accounts count for less, because their value can drop and withdrawals can be taxed. Here is how one of our lenders counts them:

Type of accountHow much counts
Checking, savings, money market100%
Money from selling real estate you owned100%
Stocks, bonds, mutual funds70%
Retirement accounts, if you are 59½ or older70%
Retirement accounts, if you are under 59½60%

Fannie Mae's version is stricter. It counts only retirement accounts and a retirement or severance payout from an employer. Money from selling a business or a house does not count under Fannie Mae's rules, but it does with lenders like the one above.

Asset depletion loan requirements

Every lender sets its own rules. These are typical, from one of the lenders we work with:

  • Enough assets. At least $1 million, or 150% of the loan amount, whichever is lower. This minimum doesn't apply if you are using your assets to add to other income, like Social Security or a pension.
  • Seasoned money. The money has been in a U.S. account for at least 120 days. Money from selling real estate you owned doesn't need to wait.
  • Recent statements. Your 4 most recent monthly statements, recent quarterly statements, or a verification form from your bank.
  • Money you can reach. The accounts must be available to you without a penalty.
  • Everyone on the loan. Anyone named on the accounts must also sign the loan.
  • The lower credit score. If two of you apply, the lender uses the lower of your scores.

Can you combine it with Social Security or a pension?

Yes. Your asset income is added to your Social Security, pension or other income, and the lender looks at the total. With that lender, the $1 million minimum is waived when your assets are only adding to other income.

Do you have to sell your investments?

No. The lender only needs to see that the money is yours and that you can reach it. Your accounts can stay invested. The formula is a way to measure what you can afford, not a plan to drain your savings.

Asset depletion or a bank statement loan?

If you are self-employed and your business deposits are steady, a bank statement loan may fit better. It looks at the money flowing through your accounts each month. Asset depletion looks at the money sitting in them. If you are buying a rental, a DSCR loan qualifies you on the rent instead. Asset depletion loan questions

What is an asset depletion loan?

An asset depletion loan is a mortgage where the lender turns your savings and investments into a monthly income figure, so you can qualify without a paycheck. It is often used by retirees and people who sold a business.

How is asset depletion income calculated?

The lender takes your eligible assets, subtracts the down payment, closing costs and required reserves, and divides the rest by a set number of months. Fannie Mae uses the months in the loan, 360 for a 30-year mortgage. Some lenders divide by as few as 60 months.

Can I get a mortgage with no income but assets?

Yes. With an asset depletion loan, your savings and investments can stand in for income. You'll need enough assets left after the purchase, and the money usually needs to have been in your account for a few months.

Do retirement accounts count for asset depletion?

Yes, usually at part of their value. One of our lenders counts 70% of a retirement account if you are 59½ or older and 60% if you are younger. Cash in checking or savings counts in full.

Sources

  • Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-3.4-06, Employment-Related Assets as Qualifying Income
